title: August Stock Pick: Everybody Is Watching The Wrong Number
description: The whole debate is about one line in the accounts. The money gets decided on a different one.
body_html:
Some of you will recall that last December I took my family to Chile, and we only made it back to Toronto in April. Besides avoiding the Canadian winter, we had a long list of things to sort out down there. One of them was my mom’s back surgery.

You might ask why she didn’t have the surgery in Canada. I am covered as a Canadian citizen, my mom isn’t, and there is no private hospital system here to fall back on. So for years I have been paying for a private health plan for her in Chile for exactly this kind of situation, and this was her third back surgery. On top of the private plan I carry a complementary policy for her as well. In a nutshell, on a $55,000 surgery at Chilean prices, I paid the $1,902 deductible and nothing else.

Why am I talking about this and how is it relevant to the August stock pick?

Between Chile, Canada and the years I spent in the US, I have dealt with health care systems that run from public to private to barely there. Health care touches all of us at some point in our lives, so why not our portfolios!

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • How the pick ranks

  • From a whiteboard in 2012 to three million members

  • How this industry actually makes money

  • The market really is shrinking

  • The line nobody models

  • The capital question nobody asks

  • Management and capital allocation

  • Valuation

  • Steel-manning the bear

  • What Mr. Market is missing

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • OSCR grew membership +46% y/y into a market that shrank 12%. Revenue grew +70% y/y in Q2 and the overhead ratio fell 450bp to a company record.

  • The debate everybody is having is about the medical loss ratio. The line that moves the profit and loss is the ACA risk adjustment transfer, which took a fifth of direct premium in H1.

  • That transfer gets bigger, mechanically, every time OSCR wins share by being the cheapest plan on the exchange.

  • OSCR earns a trailing ROE of 38.5%. Quota share reinsurance makes this far more capital-light than the market prices it as.

  • The key risk is a post-subsidy risk pool that is sicker than OSCR priced for, and 2027 is when that shows up. H2 2026 guidance already implies an operating loss.

  • Fair value $42 against $28, bear case $21. Risk and reward of 1 to 2. BUY.

How the pick ranks

Valuation 26. Almost every metric has a strong score, except for P/E, P/B and the dividend yield, since it doesn’t pay a dividend. Interesting that the trailing P/E is lower than the forward P/E (15.5x vs. 24.1x). Mr. Market is paying less for what OSCR has already earned than for what it is about to earn, which tells you consensus has H2 2026 earnings collapsing.

They do, and I will get to why.

Growth 97. Trailing revenue, EBITDA, EBIT and EPS growth all rank in the top decile, while forward EBIT and EBITDA growth rank at the very bottom of the peer set. The trailing column is the 2026 recovery. The forward column is the guided H2 trough sitting inside the next twelve months of estimates. Same split as the valuation factor, same cause.

Profitability 77. Every margin metric ranks in the bottom quartile of financials and every return metric ranks in the top decile. A 3.6% net income margin producing a 38.5% ROE is the thesis in two numbers: OSCR earns thin margins on an enormous revenue base and almost no equity, which is what a well-run insurer looks like. Ignore the negative ROIC, invested capital goes negative when a company holds more float than capital.

Sentiment 98 and Outlook 89. Both reflect a share price that has roughly doubled since April and a rising consensus estimate behind it.

Look at who OSCR screens next to. Hinge Health [], Kymera [], Immunovant [], and only Alignment Healthcare [] is an actual insurance company. The screen sorted OSCR into high-growth healthcare instead of into managed care with UnitedHealth [], Elevance [], Centene [] and Molina []. That is a clue about how Mr. Market currently thinks about this name, and I think it is the wrong bucket.

You can run the same work on any ticker yourself at RankedStocks.com, free.

From a whiteboard in 2012 to three million members

Two people started OSCR in 2012, Mario Schlosser and Joshua Kushner, and the pitch was that health insurance in America is a technology problem. Build the claims engine, the member app, the billing system and the provider data layer yourself instead of licensing forty years of somebody else’s mainframe, and you should be able to run the same book of business for less.

It went public in March 2021 at $39 a share. OSCR lost $571M in 2021, $610M in 2022, $271M in 2023, made $26M in 2024, then lost $443M again in 2025.

Five years, one profitable one.

That 2025 loss is the scar everybody still points at. The MLR went from 81.7% to 87.4%, and Q4 alone printed 95.4%. Two things happened at once: the market got sicker than anybody had priced, and OSCR’s own members looked healthier relative to that sicker market.

Along the way the business got narrower and better. OSCR tried Medicare Advantage and exited before plan year 2024, having reached the grand total of 3,864 members. It tried small group through a Cigna partnership and let it lapse at the end of 2024. It left California. What survives is one product in one market, ACA individual health plans, sold in 20 states for 2026, plus a distribution layer it bought in 2025 (an enrolment platform, an insurance agency, and a lead generation site).

The other thing that changed was the CEO. Mark Bertolini arrived in April 2023, and if you don’t follow US healthcare, the short version is that he ran Aetna for eight years and sold it to CVS [] for $69B. In April 2026 he put $11.92M of his own money into a million shares at $11.92, bought straight from the company at the previous day’s closing price. No discount.

By the way, now in RankedStocks.com you can track insiders transactions (go to the Research -> Trades tab)

598,000 at the end of 2021, just over a million in 2022, a dip to 1.04M in 2023 after the exits, then 1.68M, then 2.04M, and then 3.4M signed up during the 2026 open enrolment period, settling at 2.96M effectuated members by June.

It is concentrated: at the end of 2025 Florida was 57.8% of members, Texas 17.6% and Georgia 10.7%. And OSCR, a company that calls itself a technology company, owned zero issued patents as of December 2025.

How this industry actually makes money

If you already know how ACA plans work, skip ahead. If you don’t, most of the mistakes in the published commentary on this company come from the mechanics below.

Where the money comes from. An American who doesn’t get health insurance through an employer and isn’t old enough for Medicare buys a plan on an exchange, which is a government-run website. Plans come in metal tiers (catastrophic, bronze, silver, gold, platinum) that differ in how much of each medical bill the member pays before the insurer starts paying.

Here is the part that surprises people. 93% of OSCR’s premium comes directly from the federal government and 7% comes from the members. Most enrollees qualify for an Advance Premium Tax Credit, a subsidy CMS pays straight to the insurer on their behalf. So this is a business whose customer chooses the product and whose payer is the US Treasury.

Those subsidies were temporarily enhanced from 2021 through 2025, which took premiums to zero for anyone under 150% of the federal poverty level and capped everyone else at 8.5% of income. The enhancements expired on 31 December 2025. The entire industry debate for two years has been about what happens next.

Where the money goes. Three places, and you need all three.

Claims. The medical loss ratio, or MLR, is claims divided by premium. At an 80% MLR, 80 cents of every premium dollar goes back out as medical bills. Federal law sets a minimum: an individual-market insurer running below an 80% MLR has to rebate the difference to its members, and New York requires 82%. So the MLR has a floor as well as a ceiling, and any bull case built on OSCR running a 70% MLR forever is a bull case that hasn’t read the rulebook.

Overheads. SG&A. For OSCR this covers commissions to the brokers who bring in the members, premium taxes and exchange fees, the quota share reinsurance fee, and everything else. The technology story shows up here or it shows up nowhere.

The risk adjustment transfer. A payment insurers make to each other, based on how sick their members are relative to everybody else’s in the same state. It took a fifth of direct premium in H1.

Why profits are front-loaded inside the year. Premium arrives level, twelve months a year. But the member pays the deductible first. In January the member is covering most of each bill; by October the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum are exhausted and the insurer is paying nearly all of it. So the MLR is structurally lowest in Q1 and highest in Q4, and reported earnings are heavily front-loaded. An insurer that makes a fortune in H1 and loses money in H2 hasn’t deteriorated as it is the nature of the business. Hold that thought, because it is the whole explanation for the number that scared Mr. Market six weeks ago.

How the capital works. An insurance subsidiary has to hold statutory capital against the risk it writes, set by risk-based capital rules. Cash sitting in a subsidiary needs a regulator’s blessing before it can move up to the parent. And insurers can rent capital instead of owning it, through quota share reinsurance, where a reinsurer takes a fixed percentage of the premiums and the matching percentage of the claims, which shrinks the capital the insurer has to hold against the business. OSCR ceded 47% of premium this way in 2025.

The market really is shrinking

The bear on this stock has the facts on his side.

The enhanced subsidies are gone. KFF’s work shows out-of-pocket premium payments more than doubling on average once the enhancements come off…

… and average monthly effectuated marketplace enrolment falling toward 17.5M in 2026 from 22.3M in 2025. The Urban Institute puts coverage losses at 7.3M people. OSCR’s own read at Q2 was a market of 19.2M lives, down 12% y/y.

The average hides who actually gets hit. The burden climbs with income all the way to the subsidy cliff, and the household just above four times the poverty line loses the credit outright and eats the gross premium increase on top of that. Which of those two households renews in January is the whole question.

It gets harder from here. The 2027 rate filings are in, and they are double digits again.

That is the second consecutive year, with four percentage points of it attributed specifically to the sicker pool left behind after the subsidies lapsed. The 2027 open enrolment window shortens back to 1 November through mid-December, and the 2027 payment notice reinstates stricter income verification. Every one of those changes takes lives out of the pool.

So there’s a real question here, and the most-read bear piece on OSCR makes it the whole thesis: how do you own a share gainer in a market that is contracting?

The answer is to look at what the contraction is doing to the competition. MOH is cutting its ACA book to six states from fourteen and expects about $1B less in ACA premium next year, CNC drops exchange coverage in Delaware and New Hampshire at the end of 2026, and Cigna [] leaves the individual exchange in all eleven of its states for 2027. The trade press now describes the sector’s stance as profitability over membership. OSCR’s share across its own footprint went from 17% in 2025 to 30% in 2026. When a market shrinks 12% and your book grows 46%, somebody handed you those members.

There is also a second market forming underneath this one that most of the OSCR commentary treats as a footnote. ICHRA lets an employer hand each employee a fixed pot of money to buy an individual plan instead of running a group scheme. More than 20,000 US businesses now offer one, membership grew 124% y/y from 2024 to 2025, fewer than 10% of employers who adopt it go back, and two thirds of the small businesses adopting it were offering no coverage at all before. Oliver Wyman has published an insurer playbook for exactly this disruption.

ICHRA gets no number in my model. Nobody can size it credibly yet and OSCR doesn’t break it out. But the shrinking-market bear case assumes the addressable population is capped by ACA enrolment, and ICHRA is the mechanism by which that stops being true. Free optionality in a thesis that doesn’t need it.

The line nobody models

The ACA has a mechanism called risk adjustment, and it exists to stop insurers competing by cherry-picking healthy customers. Inside each state, every insurer’s members get a risk score based on their demographics and their diagnoses. Insurers whose members score below the state average write a cheque into a pool. Insurers whose members score above it get paid out of that pool. The pool sums to zero within each state. No government money goes in or comes out. It is a transfer between competitors.

The size of your cheque is your risk-score gap multiplied by the statewide average premium. So the amount owed has nothing to do with your claims, or your premiums, or how well you ran the business. It depends on how your members’ recorded health compares to everybody else’s in that state.

Here is what that meant for OSCR. The risk adjustment transfer payable was $2.6B at the end of 2025 against $11.7B of revenue, and by 30 June 2026 the net payable had grown to $4.8B. In H1 2026 the transfer ran at 20% of direct policy premium. That is a bigger line than SG&A. It is the largest deduction from revenue after claims themselves, and it never appears as an expense, because it nets straight out of premium revenue before you ever see it.

The bear case should be built here rather than on the subsidy story. OSCR wins members by being the cheapest plan on the exchange. Cheap plans attract younger, healthier, lower-utilizing people. Healthy members produce a low risk score. A low risk score means a bigger cheque into the pool. The shift into bronze and high-deductible plans that flattered the MLR in H1 also suppressed the risk score that sets the transfer.

Which is precisely what went wrong in 2025. In Q2 and Q3 the market’s average risk score came in far above expectation, so the denominator moved against OSCR. Then in Q4 third-party reports showed OSCR’s own relative risk scores were lower than anticipated, so the numerator moved against it as well. Both directions cost money, in the same year.

Three more things about this line.

It is a guess until June of the following year. OSCR does not know what it owes. It estimates its own risk scores from lagged claims data, it estimates the market average from third-party surveys, and CMS doesn’t publish the real answer until roughly twelve months in arrears. The auditors designated the valuation of this payable a critical audit matter and brought in specialists to test it. When you read a quarterly MLR from this company, you are reading an estimate wrapped around a number nobody will know for a year.

It is where the technology story should show up, and nobody checks. If OSCR’s platform genuinely produces better clinical documentation and more accurate diagnosis coding, the payoff lands here. Watch whether the transfer as a percentage of direct premium falls through 2027 while membership keeps growing.

It is calculated state by state. The transfer runs against a statewide average premium, in each state separately. OSCR has 57.8% of its members in Florida. Its risk adjustment economics are, to a first approximation, a bet on the composition of one state’s risk pool.

So when the H1 numbers landed and the bulls celebrated a 75.0% MLR, they were reading half the equation. And when the bears point at the FY2025 87.4% MLR as proof the business can’t underwrite, they are reading the same half. The MLR is the number the industry reports. The transfer decides who keeps the money.

The capital question nobody asks

OSCR has $8.6B of cash & equivalents on its balance sheet.

That $8.6B isn’t OSCR’s money in any useful sense. Most of it is float, premium collected in advance against claims not yet paid, sitting alongside $6.1B of payables owed to CMS as at June.

The number that matters is how much capital OSCR has to keep locked up to write the business, and the answer is remarkably little.

The CFO gave the rule of thumb on the Q4 call: for every $1B of premium, OSCR holds roughly $50M of capital, and that already reflects a 55% quota share ceding rate for 2026. Five cents of capital per premium dollar. Without the reinsurance, the subsidiaries would have needed an extra $683.1M at the end of 2025, and roughly $1.1B by June 2026. So OSCR is renting a large slice of its regulatory capital and paying the fee out of SG&A, where it sits invisible inside the overhead ratio everybody praises.

Stack that against the earnings and you get the 38.5% ROE that ranks in the top decile of financials. A business earning a 3.6% net margin on ten cents of equity per dollar of revenue is a business earning a very high return on equity.

The capital position has also swung hard, in OSCR’s favour. Statutory capital and surplus at the subsidiaries went from $1.2B at the end of 2024 to $1.0B at the end of 2025 (the loss year ate it) and then to $1.9B by June 2026. Excess capital above the regulatory minimum went $734M, then $315M, then $994M. The parent pulled $300M of dividends out of the subsidiaries in H1 and used it to fund a new Florida entity.

So here is the question for 16 September, when OSCR holds its 2026 Investor Day. What happens to $994M of excess capital? There is no buyback authorization, there is no dividend, and there has never been either. My base case assumes OSCR starts paying out a rising share of earnings from 2028, reaching 65% by the end of the decade, because a business needing five cents of capital per premium dollar can’t sensibly retain everything it makes. If that is wrong and the money simply piles up, the equity base balloons, ROE falls mechanically, and my fair value comes down by roughly $4.

I think that is the most important unanswered question on this name.

Management and capital allocation

The CEO has been in the job for three years, and the record is mixed in a way I find reassuring. He exited Medicare Advantage, exited small group, exited California, and cut the state count from 22 to 18 before rebuilding to 20. Shrinking a business down to one product is a strategy I like; it reminds me of Jack Welch at GE, where every business had to be number one or number two in its market or it got fixed, sold or closed.

On pricing the discipline has been real, and it predates the crisis. OSCR has assumed the enhanced subsidies would expire since its 2024 investor day and priced accordingly. For 2026 it filed a weighted average increase of 28% into a market where some competitors pushed far higher, and grew 46% anyway. It also priced for a 20% to 30% market contraction, towards the high end of that band, and the contraction has come in at 12%.

Where I would push back is on disclosure. The Q2 guidance raise was $250M and favourable prior-period development through six months was $232M, of which $160M was a single prior-year risk adjustment true-up. When an analyst put that arithmetic to management on the call, the answer conceded the maths and pivoted to “more tailwinds than headwinds.” Core operations contributed perhaps $18M of the raise.

The capital structure is clean. $431.6M of convertible notes, $410M of it at 2.25% due 2030 with a $24.82 conversion price, and $35M at 7.25% due 2031. The 2030 notes met their conversion condition in Q2, so 20.7M shares are now sitting in the diluted count. A $475M revolving facility was put in place in February 2026 and remains undrawn. Against $10.2B of cash and investments and $1.9B of statutory surplus, the balance sheet isn’t the risk here.

One governance item you should price. Joshua Kushner, through the Thrive Capital funds, owns 14.2% of the company and controls 68.0% of the votes, because his 32.9M Class B shares carry 20 votes each. It makes OSCR a controlled company under NYSE rules, although it has not taken up any of the governance exemptions that status allows.

Valuation

I value insurers on excess return. An insurer’s earnings are a function of the capital it is required to hold, so the honest question is what it earns on that capital above what the capital costs.

The model runs a cost of equity of 8.0%, built from a 4.72% risk-free rate, a 4.23% equity risk premium and a beta of 0.77. That beta comes from Damodaran’s January 2026 Healthcare Support Services set, relevered for OSCR’s capital structure. OSCR’s own shares are far more volatile than 0.77 implies, and most of that volatility is US health policy, which is idiosyncratic and doesn’t belong in a beta.

Base case fair value is $42. It assumes revenue of $18.85B in 2026, the midpoint of guidance, growing to $34.7B by 2035, a compound rate below 7% and well under the 20% management has talked about. It assumes the operating margin reaches management’s 5% target in 2030 rather than 2027. It assumes tax stays near zero for two more years while the net operating losses run off, then normalizes to 23%. And it assumes the capital return I described above.

Those assumptions produce 2027 EPS of $2.11, just under management’s stated 2027 target of $2.25, and 2030 EPS of $2.86. At $42 you would be paying 15x that.

Removing CNC, MOH and CLOV from the managed health care space (as they have returned negative ROE)…

… we are left with six companies in the space. Save for ELV, they all trade higher than OSCR while they have lower ROEs.

The bull case at $63 has the market stabilizing near 19M lives, ICHRA becoming a real revenue line, and OSCR hitting the 5% margin on the original timeline before pushing to 6%. The bear case at $21 has 2027 as an accident year, with the operating margin dropping to 1.5% as the risk pool bites, revenue falling two years running, and a slow recovery on a smaller base.

At $28 the upside to base is $14 and the downside to bear is $7. Risk and reward of 1 to 2. That ratio describes the shape of the payoff if my range is right, and the range is only as good as the bear case, which is next.

Run the model 10,000 times with those assumptions varying and 82% of the outcomes land above today’s share price. That matters more to me than any single point estimate, because it says the thesis does not need my base case to be right, only for it not to be badly wrong.

The spread on the payout ratio is the honest part of this. A 20 point standard deviation around a 45% mean is enormous, and it is there because OSCR has never returned a dollar of capital and nobody outside the company knows what it will do with the $994M sitting at the subsidiaries. Cost of equity and terminal growth barely move the answer by comparison.

Steel-manning the bear

First, the H2 arithmetic. OSCR earned $1.1B of operating profit in H1 and guides to $500M-$700M for the full year. That implies an operating loss of $400M-$600M in H2, on unchanged revenue guidance, with the implied H2 MLR running near 88-89% against 75.0% in H1. My explanation is deductible seasonality, plus an enormous cohort of brand new members who haven’t yet started using their benefits, plus conservatism. The bear’s explanation is that management can see something in the claims data that we can’t. Both explanations fit the guidance. Only one of them explains why the company raised it.

Second, and this is the one that would actually cost me money, the 2027 risk pool. Insurers filing 2027 rates are explicitly citing a sicker residual pool as the reason for four points of the increase. OSCR grew 46% into a shrinking market by being cheap. If the people it collected are sicker than it priced for, the MLR rises and the risk adjustment transfer won’t fall to offset it, because the transfer depends on relative scores across the whole state rather than on OSCR’s own claims. That is a two-sided squeeze and it is exactly what produced the 2025 loss. FY2025 happened once already, and nothing structural prevents it happening again.

Third, the raise was borrowed from last year. $232M of the $250M came from prior-period development. Strip it out and the core 2026 operating margin sits near 2% against the 3.2% the guide midpoint implies, so my path to 5% starts from a lower base than the headline suggests.

Fourth, concentration. Florida is 57.8% of the book. A bad hurricane season, a state regulatory change, or an adverse shift in one state’s risk pool hits OSCR harder than it hits any diversified insurer, and three hospital systems account for 24% of allowable medical costs between them.

Fifth, the MLR floor. Any model with OSCR running below an 80% MLR for a sustained period is a model that owes members a rebate. Underwriting alone can only make this business so profitable, and everything past that point has to come from overheads and scale.

Then the thing that is less a risk than a condition of ownership. This is a business whose revenue is 93% a federal transfer payment, in a policy area that moves with every administration and is currently the subject of active litigation. There is no version of this investment where you aren’t exposed to Washington.

What Mr. Market is missing

Three things, in order of what I think they are worth.

The first is what this whole thesis has been about. The published debate is a referendum on the MLR and on subsidies, while the risk adjustment transfer is a larger line that behaves differently and gets almost no coverage. Until people model it, they will keep being surprised in both directions, celebrating a Q1 MLR that was flattered by a mix shift which raises next year’s transfer, then panicking at a Q4 true-up that was baked in eighteen months earlier.

The second is that Mr. Market is valuing OSCR as a high-growth healthcare story when it should be valued as an insurer. A forward P/E of 24.1x on a guided trough year is close to meaningless for a business whose earnings are seasonally front-loaded and whose largest deduction from revenue is an estimate. Value it on what it earns against the capital it is required to hold and a 38.5% ROE against an 8% cost of equity is a franchise.

The third is the capital itself. Nearly a billion dollars of excess capital at the subsidiaries, in a business that consumes five cents of capital per premium dollar, with no buyback and no dividend and an investor day in five weeks.

Verdict

BUY, fair value $42. OSCR goes in as the August monthly pick.

What I keep coming back to is that the market handed this company three million members while its competitors were retreating, and the debate is still about whether it can control its claims. On the evidence it probably can. But the number that decides whether this investment works is a transfer payment between competitors that settles a year in arrears, and the one asset that might give OSCR a real edge on it is the diagnosis coding engine everybody keeps describing as an app.

Watch the September investor day. If you found this useful, send it to someone who owns health insurers.
